                                                                                    REPORT
CEMENT INDUSTRY — AN INTRODUCTION
1.1       There was a wide gap between the demand and supply of cement during the Seventies. During that time the
major cement units were not motivated either to produce to their full capacity or to expand as cement production was
under both price and distribution control i.e., their entire production was under levy obligation on the rate fixed by the
government from time to time.
1.2       The then Central Government had been considering various measures for achieving rapid increase in the
production of cement by establishing a large number of mini cement units, as in the case of China, where it was found
that the working of mini cement units are highly successful.
1.3       In the existing situation, a perception grew that establishment of mini cement plants would usher in an era
resulting in exploitation of smaller limestone deposits, dispersal of cement production capacity all over the country,
reduction of burden on the railway, lower capital cost and quicker installation and higher employment especially in
rural, hilly and other inaccessible areas. The then Government accordingly constituted two working groups to make
suitable recommendations regarding the choice of technology, and provision for fiscal incentives to attract large number
of entrepreneurs to this field.
Criteria for Mini Cement Plants
2.1       The Government considered the reports of both the working groups and announced the following decisions in
their press release No. 9-98/78 Cem dated 4.1.1979 :-
                 1.  The capacity for the mini cement plant will be limited to 200 tonnes per day on 66000 tonnes per annum.
                 2.  The choice of technology to be utilised should be left to the entrepreneurs.
                 3.  In addition to the units which may be set up by the entrepreneurs in the private sector or by the State
Government in the joint sector, the Cement Corporation of India would also enter the field to set up mini
cement plants as a promotional effort.
                 4.  The ex-works price of cement produced by the mini cement plants would be the same as the price
admissible to new large sized plants, viz. Rs. 296 per tonne. This price was assured for a period of five
years from the date of going into commercial production.
                 5.  Mini cement plants will be allowed a rebate in the payment for a period of five years.
                 6.  While the mini cement plants will be subject to price control under the Cement Control Order, they will be
exempted from distribution control under the same order.
                 7.  Mini cement plants set up in hilly and remote areas will be eligible for additional excise duty relief and
cash subsidy on merit.
                 8.  Mini cement plants will also be eligible for all other existing incentives and facilities available under the
Income Tax Act or under other schemes offered by the State Government.
                 9.  Large houses and foreign majority companies will not be allowed to set up mini cement plants.

2.2       Taking a cue from the above Government notification and announcement made by the Central Government in
the 8th Five Year Plan about building of infrastructure in the country, 126 mini cement plants were set up in the State of
Uttar Pradesh to supply the much needed cement for the various projects. But due to variety of reasons, these units
became sick and unviable.
Study made by the Sub-Committee for the Ministry of Small Scale Industries

Committee on Industry decided to study the problem faced by the mini cement plants in UP. The Sub-Committee
consisted of the following Members :

Meeting with the Mini Cement Plants Association
            The sub-committee had a meeting with the U.P. Mini Cement Plants Association on 4th June 2002. The
morandum submitted by the Association is reproduced below: -
                 (i)  Almost all mini cement units in the State have been closed because the guarantee given to provide
government protection to these units has not been fulfilled either by the State government or by the so call
Industries friend "Udyog Bandhu". This fact is known to one and all that no such decision has been taken
by UP Finance Corporation, Industrial Directorate and the "Udyog Bandhu" during the last four years after
much deliberations which could help the said units to revive while on the other hand, Rajasthan Finance
Corporation by making into account the seriousness of the situation, had taken a quick decision not only to
waive the interest completely but waived 20 per cent principal amount also so that mini cement units
situated in Rajasthan may be revived.
                (ii)  The Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation which on the one hand had the survey conducted by the ICRA for
the small cement industries falling on the verge of closure and sought suggestions for the revival thereof,
turned down the proposals made by the ICRA completely to be implemented. The letter of the MD,
Finance Corporation, in this regard is enclosed (Annexure–I).
               (iii)  Whereas the said issue was approved to be decided by the High Power Committee headed by the Chief
Minister (Annexure II) on the one hand, the Udyog Bandhu did not feel it pertinent to include the same in
the meeting of the High Power Committee, on the other hand. The letter forwarded by the Association in

               (iv)  On the one hand, Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation has accepted in its report that out of 48 units, 46 are
sick while on the other hand it has started the process of harassment against these units instead of reviving
them. As a result thereof, remaining units are also closing (Report of Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation
Annexure–IV).
                (v)  Taking inspiration from press release No. 9-98/78 cement dated January 4, 1979 
(Annexure–V) by Central Government and Eighth Five Year Plan, State Government had invited
entrepreneurs for setting up small cement units. The aim of Central Government behind this was that with
the setting up of these industries, small deposits of limestone will be utilised where it is not possible to set
up big units. On the other hand, on the basis of resolution adopted by the Central Government during the
said Five Year Plan that for construction of 20000 km double express highway, two million houses, target
to generate 1 lakh megawatt power and construction of 12000 km highway and urgent requirement of
cement, it was decided that the said target can be met only when small units of cement are set up under the
protection of Government and supply of cement is taken from the said small units of cements because it
would have taken 5 to 6 years for getting cement as per production capacity of big units.
               (vi)  Central Government had also kept it in mind that small producers of cement requires less capital as
compared to big producer of cement and setting up expenditure per ton will also be less, employment
opportunities will increase and the main thing was that small scale industries will develop and the country
will be prosperous.
                      Review statement regarding causes of Small Scale Industries getting sick :-
                         (i)  The interest rate was fixed at 13.5 per cent per annum at the time of sanctioning financial assistance
by the Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation to these small units but after investing margin money and
complying with all the formalities such as NOC from Pollution Control Board and letter of sanction
regarding power from the Power Corporation by these industries, it has been fixed @ 19.75 per cent
at the time of getting loan and before taking such step no consideration has been made with regard to
the future of these units and ultimately all the units have come under the burden of credit and became
almost closed.
                        (ii)  In 1996-97, Hon'ble Supreme Court banned the mining of limestone. As a result thereof supply of
major raw material i.e. limestone had stopped and self-producing capacity of units of making clinker
vanished.
                       (iii)  126 small cement units in which 50 per cent have the capacity to produce clinker, have completely
vanished due to further enhancement in production vis-a-vis its demand and decrease in purchase of
cement by the Government and no increase in the price of cement since last eight years in the State
and remaining units are doing only grinding by purchasing clinker from big units.
                       (iv)  Large scale units have been exempted from sales tax for 12 years for establishing industry in Uttar
Pradesh and consequently, large scale cement manufacturing units like Satna, ACC, have established
and still establishing their new grinding units in Uttar Pradesh. These units manufacture cement after
grinding the clinker and they get clinker from their parent unit which is situated in other States.
Therefore, they get exemption from sales tax from one State owing to the manufacture of clinker and
on the other hand after showing the transfer of clinker stock to other State they get exemption from
sales tax owing to the manufacture of cement. Due to this double relaxation, the sale price of their
cement is less because of low production cost and no burden of sales tax, whereas small scale
industries have been exempted from sales tax only for two years and because of this injustice, the
small scale industries of cement are adversely affected in the State.
                        (v)  It is clear from the above-mentioned explanation that small scale industries which are on the verge of
closure, and are doing only grinding work, pay the sales tax to the State at the rate of 12.5 per cent for
manufacturing cement by taking clinker from these large scale industries. Thus these small-scale
industries pay total 12.5 + 4 = 16.5 per cent sales tax whereas large scale industries sell their cement

are those whose promoters could get relief from the Finance Corporation by paying under lump sum
scheme in pressure of penalty action by the Finance Corporation despite the fact that these units are
closed. 13 units are those units which are on the verge of being closed (Annexure VI and VII).
                       (xi)  In view of the above mentioned problems and adverse circumstances, a study was got done by Uttar
Pradesh Finance Corporation through ICRA to find out the reasons of failure of small scale industrial
units and measures for their revival. They have categorically made by the following suggestions in
their report for the revival of the said industrial units :

PRAYER
            If the Government is interested in running these industries in the state in order to provide employment and
assistance to the Government in manufacturing work in the national interest, and thereby making the State self-
dependent, the following measures must be considered:
                 (i)  If compliance of suggestions made by ICRA with respect of 13 units as mentioned in Annexure-VII is
ensured and the interest due on the said units is waived, Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation would not only
receive Rs. 15,02,59,415/- but also the said 13 units would also get revived.
                (ii)  Small scale cement units would not be able to compete with big units unless they are fully exempted from
sales tax, as suggested by ICRA since larger units are enjoying exemption from sales tax for the last 12
years.
               (iii)  Public Sector Undertakings should ensure purchase preference and imposition of 15% price preference.
Besides all Government Departments should be directed to meet their entire cement requirement first from

5.         Committee's findings, observations and recommendations
5.1       Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation made a study regarding mini cement plants financed by the Corporation. The
study report inter-alia  mentioned that the performance of the cement industry is closely linked with the industrial
growth of the country. In the period from 1993-94 to 1995-96, when the industrial growth was higher, the scenario in
the segment was bright. In 1995-96 with 11.7% industrial growth, the cement production grew at 10.6%. As the industry
slowed down in 1996-97, so did the cement segment. The same downward trend continued in 1998-99. According to the
industry sources, the current take-off position is inadequate to generate more profits, as the low price realisation is still
not matching the production cost. The recession in construction activity, low investment in major infrastructure projects,
rise in the cost of power cost etc. coupled with high borrowing cost has marked down the industry's earnings.
5.2       Another major constraint in this segment is excess capacity. During the growth phase of the industry, almost all
major players in this sector had gone for huge capacity addition. As a result, the installed capacity of cement industry
doubled in the last four years. In 1996-97 the installed capacity was 96.25 million tonnes, going up to 105.25 million
tonnes in 1997-98. Some additional capacity is still expected to be installed in the coming years. Due to the huge
capacity available with major plants, they have encroached upon the segment of the mini cement plants by entering the
remotest areas. Mini cement plants, which traditionally used to cater to the local markets of remote areas, were
therefore, badly affected.
5.3       The study report further mentioned that the immediate future is not very encouraging. However, once the
Government starts the revival of the economy through investment in infrastructure and construction activity picks up,
the demand for cement will grow.
5.4       The Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation also entrusted ICRA with the job of preparing a report on the cement
sector. The ICRA had cited high interest rate charged by Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation as one of the problems
faced by the SSI units in cement sectors.
5.5       The Committee observes that the State Government had revised the rate of interest from 13.5% to 19.75% in
1991-92. The reasons for charging high rate of interest by Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation was due to the fact that it
got loans from SIDBI/IDBI at a higher rate. The Committee, however, feels that revising the rate of interest was not in
the interest of mini cement plants. The Government should have calculated the viability of those projects before revising
the rate of interest as it proved a disincentive for SSIs in the cement sector. As regards giving loans by SIDBI/IDBI on
higher rate of interest to Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation, the Committee observes that the U.P. Administration with
SIDBI/IDBI should have sorted out the matter.
5.6       The Committee notes that SSIs engaged in this business took loans from the financial institutions/banks, but due
to industrial slow down and stiff competition from giant plants they have to dispose of their products through distress
sale, which contributed to accumulation of interest against the principal amount of loan. Rising of interest by
Government under such circumstances proved to be the death knell for the SSIs in the cement sector. The Committee
further notes that Rajasthan Financial Corporation, under a one-time settlement, not only waived the interest completely
but also waived 20% principal amount so that the mini cement units situated in Rajasthan may survive.
5.7       In comparison, the units of Uttar Pradesh are working in a climate of apathy. Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation,
in a letter dated 4.10.2000 addressed to "Udyog Bandhu" (A Forum of Industrial Associations), mentioned that the
members of the mini cement plants association desired that whatever repayment (by way of interest or repayment) they
have made till date to the corporation may be adjusted towards principal and balance may be recovered from them in
easy instalments. The Board had already rejected this proposal earlier. However, if there is any demand of the
association for waiver of total or part of interest, the same is to be taken to the Board again for its approval.
5.8       The Committee fails to understand as to why Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation is not able to bail out the units
in UP taking a cue from the RFC when the units in UP are struggling for survival.

5.9       From the memorandum submitted by the Association, the Committee notes that problems of the units were to be
deliberated by a High Power Committee under the chairmanship of the Chief Minister. In this regard, the Directorate of
Industries, UP, in their letter dated 1.8.2000 requested Secretary, UP Administration, to place the matter before the said
High Power Committee. It appears that such a sensitive matter was not brought before that Committee. It reflects lack of
coordination between the departments of the Government. Similar situations also prevail at the central level also. On
various occasions, the Committee observed that various ministries did not have on integrated approach to solve the
problems of the industry. The Committee observes that if SSI units are to be given a boost, the different departments of
the State Government and Central Government are to work in a coordinated manner.
5.10     Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation portfolio has, at present, 48 cement-manufacturing units. Out of 48 units only
2 units are regular in payment whereas 1 unit has recently gone in production. As per the study conducted by the Uttar
Pradesh Finance Corporation, these units are facing problems relating to market recession like in transportation cost,
wage cost ban on mining, unimplemented units, temporary default, etc. The Committee notes the plethora of problems
being faced by the cement units. In the circumstances, the Committee observes that the reported harassment of these
units, instead of reviving them by the Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation, as mentioned by the Association, needs to be
looked into.
5.11     The Central Government had announced in the 8th Five Year Plan about construction of double express
highway, houses for millions, generation of power to take the electricity to the rural areas. Had such activities relating to
infrastructure building arisen, the present state of low intake of Cement would not have arisen. In fact, market demand
of cement was not in line with the Government's projection. In subsequent budgets of the Central Government the above
schemes did not find place, resulting in decline of demand of Cement.
5.12     The giant units which take 5-6 years to produce cement started production on in 1996 in UP after taking
financial assistance from IDBI on easy terms and flooded the market with cement at a cheaper rate and ousted smaller
units by waging an unfair and unequal competition. Had the development work regarding building up infrastructure
started before 1992 or during 1992-96 the smaller units would have survived and established themselves.
5.13     The Central Government had facilitated in establishing the mini cement plants to meet the demand of cement in
the emerging scenario of building up of infrastructure facilities in the country by enabling the SSI sector to get loans
from the IDBI. In all, 126 units were set up, of which 50% were in the category of integrated units (which produced
cement out of its own manufactured clinkers) and 50% were in the category of grinding units (which ground clinkers to
produce cement after purchasing clinkers from the big units). This method of producing cement by the SSI sector
received a setback when the Supreme Court banned mining of limestone and as a consequence, limestone mines were
closed in Dehradun. As a result, the supply of major raw material i.e. limestone, had stopped and self-producing
capacity of units for making clinker vanished. The remaining units are doing only grinding by purchasing clinker from
the big units. The woes of SSI sector did not end here. The capacity to produce clinker and producing cement out of
clinker has not only been taken away by the big units from the SSI sector, the price of clinker sold by them to small
units has been raised to such an extent that either the small units are unable to purchase it from big units or if they
purchase and grind them, they would not be able to sell that cement in the market because of high cost of production,
resulting in closure of mini cement plants.
5.14     Recently, the UP Government had offered 100% concession of Sales Tax for 12 years to those industries whose
investment is over PSUs crore. Under this scheme, the giant cement industries like ACC and Satna Cement have
established their grinding unit of total 8.6 lakh tonnes per annum capacity in Rai Bareily District of UP and are availing
of this concession. The State Government would lose a huge amount of revenue by granting this concession to the giant
units. The cement so produced after grinding by the giant units is much cheaper and their selling price is much lower
than that of mini plants. All the more, the giant units are availing double concessions: -
                (a)  Firstly, as a manufacturer of intermediate product i.e. clinker, they are availing sales tax exemption in
their parent state; and
                (b)  they are availing sales tax concession in UP as a manufacturer of cement.
5.15     During the course of oral evidence before the Sub-Committee, the SSI association expressed the apprehension

81st Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/81streport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:43]
that those giant industries would leave UP after 12 years and establish their units in other states to avail sales tax
concession. The Committee was informed that small units are given only two years sales tax free concession as against
12 years to the giant units.
5.16     Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation's letter dated 4th October, 2000 addressed to "Udyog Bandhu" corroborates
the above fact. The study made by ICRA had concluded that integrated mini cement units were not viable. The report
further concluded that in case the unit took up grinding function alone, the operation could become viable with some
incentives. The study had further concluded that the units could be marginally viable if they were granted total sales tax
exemption. It has been further mentioned that Government of UP had granted 12 years sales tax exemption to big units.
The revenue loss to Government from these two units along would be Rs. 345 crores. It had been reported that there was
a third new large unit coming up in the State. Revenue loss from this unit alone would be Rs. 691 crores.
5.17     The above communication is the testimony of the fact how small units are discriminated against and have been
forced to wage a battle against stronger competitors.
            When the small units were gasping for oxygen, UP government issued a circular in 1998 asking its cement
consuming departments to send their demands to small-scale industries only. In spite of this, Government departments
are not complying with the order. As a result, the order remained on paper only without any visible results. The
Committee feels that a mechanism to monitor the compliance of the Purchase Preference Policy should have been
evolved if the Government really wanted to help the SSI sector. The Committee observes that an early action to monitor
the compliance of the order even now may save the situation for the dying SSI units.
5.18     Another factor, which has crippled the mini cement plants, is the lack of credit flow to the sector. While the giant
units had no difficulty in securing loans from banks and FIs, the small units are still struggling to get loans from banks
even after the announcement made to the effect that loan would be given without any collateral security. In addition,
restriction on load carrying capacity of trucks proved to be a strangulatory provision for the mini cement plants.
6.1       In nutshell, a vision was created during the successive Five Year Plans and notifications issued in 1979 that huge
infrastructure would be created nationwide but large cement plants would not be in a position to supply the required
quantum of cement. SSI sector was encouraged to set up mini cement plants to meet the demand of additional quantum
of cement in view of its lower capital cost, quicker installation and higher employment potential coupled with the
exploitation of smaller limestone deposits by it in rural and hilly areas. The banks gave these units loan assistance and
FIs and they started setting up units when the cement industry was hailed as the harbinger of overall development of the
state. The good days for the SSI sector did not last long due to economic recession when construction activities come to
low ebb.
6.2       SSI's cup of sorrow was full when the Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation increased the rate of interest from
13.5% to 19.75% and the giant units flooded the market with their brand of cement at a much lower price than that of
mini cement plants which in turn were forced them to sell cement at a price lower than their cost of production. They
failed to pay interest on the principal amount and the banks and FIs shut their doors to these sick units.
6.3       Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation made a study about problems and possible revival scheme of mini cement
plants through ICRA, which suggested complete waiver of interest coupled with full exemption of sales tax and
imposition of 15% price preference for the revival of mini cement plants. But so far, no positive step has been taken to
save the industry.
6.4       The Committee observes that in the recent past, there has been an overall increase in the rate of growth in the
cement industry. This is an indication that construction activity has again picked up. But these activities are confined to
certain places in the country and, by and large, large industries are able to reap the benefit of such a situation. The
renewed demand for cement has not percolated to the lower level of the industry. The Committee feels a lending hand
should be given to those sick units. Ways and means should be explored to bail out them from then pathetic situation.
6.5       The Committee also notes that as per norms specified by the Reserve Bank of India, a sick unit is considered as
potentially viable, if it would be in a position, after implementing a relief package spread over a period not exceeding
five years from the commencement of the package from banks, financial institutions, Government (Central/State) and
other concerned agencies, as may be necessary, to continue to service its repayment obligations as agreed upon
including those forming part of the package, without the help of the concessions after the aforesaid period. The

6.6       In view of the RBI guidelines, the Committee recommends that Ministry of Small Scale Industries, in

attempt to revive these units keeping in view the ICRA report as well as action initiated by the Rajasthan Financial
